Varying evidence on the beneﬁcial effects of vegetables and fruits are also reported on reduced risk of diabetes. A recent meta-analysis found no signiﬁcant beneﬁt on the incidence of diabetes found with increased intakes of total fruits, or vegetables alone (Carter et al., 2010). However, the risk of diabetes was signiﬁcantly reduced by 14% large among those who consumed relatively amounts of green leafy vegetables. In another population-based, the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition in Norfolk, United Kingdom among 3,704 adults, followed-up after 11 years found that adults who consumed a diet characterized by high amounts of vegetables and fruits of 3.5 portions per day and more, with at least 12 different fruits and vegetable items in a week had signiﬁcantly a lower risk of type-II diabetes (Cooper et al., 2012). 6.3.2 Saturated fatty acids

SFAs are mainly found in animal products such as butter, cream and hard cheese and also in palm oil and coconut products. In Malaysia, palm oil is extensively used as vegetable oil in home food preparation and in the production of local biscuits, pastries and confectioneries.

--- Chunk 75 ---
in Cereals, especially whole grains are rich phytochemicals, which are natural bioactive, non- nutrient compounds regulate human physiological processes, thereby providing health beneﬁts beyond those conferred by vitamins and minerals (Cherif, 2012). Among examples of phytochemicals are polyphenols, carotenoids, phytosterols, lignans, avenanthramides and alkylresorcinols. In most cereal grains such as rice, wheat, maize, barley, oats and rye, phenolic acids are the major polyphenols contained within the bran and germ. According to Phenol-Explorer, a comprehensive database of polyphenol content, cereals and cereal-based products contain substantial amounts of polyphenols including phenolic acid and alkylphenols (Neveu et al., 2010). The amount of polyphenols in reﬁned cereals and products such as polished rice and white bread can be considered low when compared to germ and bran.

Cereal, cereal-based products and tubers provide sources of energy mainly from dietary carbohydrate and protein. Rice serves as an important source of carbohydrate in the vegetarian diet, especially among the vegans (Farmer et al., 2011; Rizzo et al., 2013). Vitamin D is an additional important nutrient for bone health because of its effects to increase the intestinal absorption of calcium. --- Chunk 93 ---
Dietary variety can be characterised by including foods from all major food groups and might be best deﬁned as simply including foods from each of the major groups. Greater diet variation is considered a “net plus” for diet quality (Kennedy, 2004). Evidence has suggested that a wide variety of plant foods can provide adequate nutrients, which is reﬂected in the

position statements of nutrition groups around the world (Melina et al., 2016; Thomas, Erdman & Burke, 2016; Agnoli et al., 2017). The dietary pattern of vegetarians was found to be of higher quality than omnivores. The vegan diet, for example, although seemingly restrictive, received the highest Healthy Eating Index (HEI-2010) and Mediterranean Diet Score (MDS) values as opposed to omnivorous diets (Clarys et al., 2014; Parker & Vadiveloo, 2019). In adults, the variety of foods consumed by the vegetarians was found to be closer to nutritional diets than recommendations (Deriemaeker et al., 2010; Clarys et al., 2013).

--- Chunk 100 ---
To protect the public against health hazards and frauds in the preparation, sale and use of foods, food manufacturers and distributors must abide by the Malaysian Food Act 1983 and Food Regulations 1985. Food labelling is an important component of the Food Act and Food Regulations. The general rules for the labelling of pre-packaged foods are laid out in Part IV (Regulation 9-18) of the Food Regulations 1985 (MOH, 1985).

In addition, food labels may provide nutrition information, some of which are mandatory. Food labels are required to provide information on the product’s nutrient content through the nutrient information panel. Labels may also carry other nutrition information such as nutrient content, nutrient function and other function claims. In addition, manufacturers may also include front-of- pack nutrition labelling. Such nutrition information helps consumers make informed choices of packaged products that can form part of an overall healthy eating plan.

Bioavailability of iron and zinc in a vegetarian diet can be increased using some food preparation techniques. Executive Summary

In recent years, there has been a global surge of interest

to adopt a vegetarian style of eating. There is no exact deﬁnition for the term vegetarian but it is commonly used to describe a plant based food diet which devoid of animal-based foods such as meat, ﬁsh and poultry. This practice has been associated with potential health beneﬁts, cultural and religious beliefs, and concern over environment and animal welfare.

Numerous studies and observations vegetarians that have generally have a higher consumption of plant foods especially fruits and vegetables, which are in phytochemicals, known to alter the risk of diet related diseases. Researchers have highlighted that vegetarians have a lower intake of cholesterol, saturated fat and total fat, and a higher intake of ﬁbre as

found

--- Chunk 108 ---
such as the Malaysian Vegetarian Society. This is based on established scientiﬁc document evidence and complements the Malaysian Dietary Guidelines 2020. The MDGV 2023 is designed in such a way that it is suitable for people with different cultural backgrounds, religions and food practices. The paramount aim of this guideline is to provide practical guidance for planning a well- balanced, plant-based diet without compromising an individual’s health.

This vegetarian dietary guideline comprises 7 key messages, with key recommendations and ‘how to achieve’ that addresses risk of nutrient deﬁciencies due to potential inadequate intakes of speciﬁc nutrients such as vitamin B12, omega-3, iron, calcium and protein. Recommendations on number of servings related to speciﬁc vegetarian food items consumed by various ethnic groups are also given in this guideline.

Foreword by Director-General of Health Ministry of Health Malaysia

The release of the Malaysian Dietary Guidelines

for Vegetarians 2023 (MDGV) is timely given that Malaysians' eating habits have changed to also include a vegetarian or plant-based diet. Despite the fact that eating and nutrition practises having altered over the past few decades, our community continues to struggle with the double burden of malnutrition and the increased prevalence of non- communicable diseases. The ﬁndings of National and Health Morbidity Survey (2019), had presented that 4.9% of Malaysia's adult population were vegetarian for a variety of reasons.

--- Chunk 110 ---
Fats, oils, sugar and salt are placed at the tip of the food pyramid. This includes ultra-processed foods which contain artiﬁcial substances such as colours, sweeteners, ﬂavours, preservatives and other additives. Fats and oils, sugars and salt are not considered food groups, but fats/ oils and especially sugar and salt, are often used during cooking or in food preparations. Vegetarians are recommended to consume these foods and ingredients the least or sparingly compared to the other food groups in the food pyramid. The recommendation for fat intake is 5 servings including nuts. However, it is well documented in the literature that excessive intake of fats/ oils, sugar and salt contributes to chronic diseases (Bowen et al., 2018). More information on fats can be found in Key Message 6.

Malaysian consumers are becoming more aware of their dietary intakes in terms of ingredients and the food additives contained therein. Hence, besides the declaration of ingredients in pre-packaged food, the law requires that food additives used in a product

be declared on the label. Any substance added to food as an additive must have been previously evaluated and approved for safety in use and controlled under the Malaysian Food Regulations 1985. Only additives in the list approved in the Food Regulations may be used.

Starting from 2024, Malaysian Food Regulations 1985 require the International Numbering System (INS) to declare food additives on the label. This is a harmonized naming system for food additives as an alternative to the use of the speciﬁc name, which may be lengthy. INS numbers are assigned to identify each food additive. INS numbers generally correspond to E numbers for the most compound, e.g. INS102, Tartrazine, is also E102.

it

Filled milk Filled milk is a product in which the milk fat has been replaced wholly or partially by an edible vegetable oil or fat, or a blend of both, such as palm oil.

Fermented milk or cultured milk Fermented milk, also known as cultured milk, is a product made by culturing pasteurised milk, sterilised milk, recombined milk, pasteurised cream or reduced cream with lactic acid bacteria. Yoghurt, cultured cream and lassi are some examples of fermented or cultured milk products.

Flavoured milk Flavored milk refers to a beverage derived from milk that incorporates approved ﬂavoring substances like chocolate, vanilla and strawberry. Typically, it contains sugar, a minimum of 2% milk fat and 8% nonfat milk solids (Food Regulations, 1985). Flavored milk undergoes a heat treatment process, either through pasteurization or ultra-high temperature treatment.

Similar effects of vegetables and fruits were also found in relation to the risk of stroke. --- Chunk 129 ---
Introduction

History of vegetarianism

Vegetarianism has a long and rich history, predating the 20th century by centuries. Its origins can be traced back to as early as the sixth century, with anthropologists suggesting that ancient humans primarily consumed a plant-based diet due to the resemblance of their digestive system to that of herbivores (Andrew et al., 2020; Philips, 2005). The practice of vegetarianism has sustained civilisations for thousands of years, driven by moral, religious, and economic factors (Hargreaves et al., 2021; Philips, 2005).

3.4.1 Areas of concern

In vegetarian diets, non-heme iron and zinc from plant sources are sensitive to inhibitors and are therefore, less bioavailable. One of the major concerns of consuming high amounts of whole grains and tubers is the reduced iron and zinc bioavailability following high intake of iron- and zinc-inhibiting components in these foods (Craig et al., 2009; Melina et al., 2016). Whole grains and tubers store phosphorus in the form of 6-phosphoinositol, better known as phytic acid or phytate, which may bind and hence inhibit the absorption of non-heme iron and zinc that are consumed concurrently (Hunt, 2002, 2003).

6.3.3 Cholesterol

Similar to saturated fats, dietary cholesterol also has an ability to alter unfavourable blood lipid levels particularly serum cholesterol and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C). A meta-analysis study reported that a reduction of over 20% in total serum cholesterol concentration can result in a 25% fall in mortality from CHD (Hooper et al., 2012). A longitudinal study of 34670 Swedish women found that greater dietary cholesterol intakes were positively associated with higher risk of cerebral infarction (RR= 1.29; 95% CI: 1.05, 1.58) (Larrson et al., 2012). The ﬁndings gathered from this review suggested that in dietary modiﬁcation, this degree of cholesterol lowering is probably beneﬁcial in reducing cardiovascular risks.

--- Chunk 140 ---
Iron is an essential component of red blood cells, and in an omnivorous diet, heme-iron derived from meat, particularly red meat, is easily absorbed by the body. However, in a vegetarian diet, heme-iron is replaced by non-heme iron obtained from sources like dried beans and peas, lentils, enriched cereals, whole-grain products, dark leafy green vegetables, and dried fruits. The bioavailability of non-heme iron depends on the balance between inhibitors (such as phytates and polyphenolics found in certain vegetables and legumes) and enhancers (such as vitamin C, citric acid, and other organic acids). To optimize iron absorption in plant-based diets, it is important to consume like legumes, whole grains, tofu, nuts, and seeds alongside foods rich in vitamin C such as guava, citrus fruits, tomatoes, cabbage, and broccoli to enhance iron absorption.

Omega-3 fatty acids are important for heart health. While ﬁsh is a common source of omega-3 fatty acids, there are vegetarian-friendly options available. Flaxseeds and ﬂaxseed oil, chia seeds, hemp seeds and walnut are excellent plant-based sources of omega-3 fatty acids. They contain alpha- linolenic acid (ALA), a type of omega-3 fatty acid. Algal oil is derived from algae and is another vegetarian source of omega-3 fatty acids, including docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) and eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA). It's important to note that while ALA can be converted to EPA and DHA in the body, the conversion rate is relatively low. However, the conversion of plant-based omega- 3 to the types used by humans is inefficient, it is, therefore, necessary for vegetarians to take fortiﬁed products or supplements, or both.

Diets that do not include ﬁsh and eggs generally lack omega-3 fatty acids, EPA and DHA, which are important for cardiovascular health and brain function (Matsumoto et al., 2019). Low dietary intakes of omega-3 fatty acids (EPA and DHA) have been observed in vegetarians, and typically none in vegans (Saunders et al., 2013). Compared with non- vegetarians, vegetarians, particularly vegans tend to have lower plasma levels of EPA and DHA (Saunders et al., 2013). Vegetarians can obtain omega-3 fatty acids from plant sources like seeds (ﬂax, chia, camelina, canola and hemp), walnuts and their oils, as well as microalgae-based DHA supplements (Saunders et al., 2013). The omega-3 fatty acid recommendation to achieve nutritional adequacy, is 0.6%-1.2% of energy for ALA; and up to 10% of this can be provided by EPA or DHA. The evidence supports a dietary recommendation of ≈500 mg/day of EPA and DHA for CVD risk reduction.

Plant-based or non-dairy milk alternatives Plant-based milk or non-dairy milk alternatives are liquids derived from plant sources. They can be categorized into different types based on the plants they are derived from, such as cereals (e.g. oat, rice, corn), legumes (e.g. soy, peanut, cowpea), nuts (e.g. almond, coconut, hazelnut, pistachio, walnut), seeds (e.g. sesame, ﬂax, sunﬂower, chia seed) and pseudo- cereals (e.g. quinoa) (Sethi et al., 2016). The nutritional composition of plant-based milk alternatives differs from that of dairy milk. However, plant-based milks fortiﬁed with protein, essential vitamins and minerals can serve as a replacement for traditional milk. As per the Food Regulation (1985), the term "milk," excluding animal-based products, can only be used for beverages derived from soybeans and coconuts.

Raw milk Raw milk is milk that has not been pasteurised or homogenised.

Low fat milk Low fat milk is milk which contains not more than 1.5 g of fat per 100 ml of milk.

2.3.2 Obesity

Epidemiologic evidence has consistently shown an inverse relationship between vegetarian diets and BMI, speciﬁcally the diet high in vegetables and fruits could help in maintaining a healthy weight and consequently prevent excessive weight gain, obesity and subsequent risk of chronic diseases. From a total of 40 studies that compared the weight status between adults who adhered to either a vegetarian or non-vegetarian (omnivorous) majority found that adults who adhered to vegetarian diet had signiﬁcantly lowered levels of BMI and/or body weight than that of their omnivorous counterparts (Berkow & Barnard, 2006). This was further supported by a recent study by Jaacks and her colleagues (2016) among vegetarian adults from Caucasian and South Asian-origns in the US which showed lowered risks of both overweight and/or obesity and abdominal obesity compared to their non-vegetarian counterparts.

Key Message 5Consume adequate amounts of milk and milk products5.1 Terminology Buttermilk Commercially available cultured buttermilk is pasteurised and homogenised with 1% to 2% fat and inoculated with bacterial culture. Buttermilk is derived from the liquid that remains after churning butter from milk cream. Condensed milk or sweetened condensed milk Condensed milk or sweetened condensed milk is produced by adding sugar to evaporated milk. It must contain a minimum of 8% milk fat and 28% milk solids (Food Regulations, 1985). Due to its high sugar content, condensed milk has a longer shelf life without the need for refrigeration. It is frequently incorporated into beverages such as coffee, tea or chocolate drinks. Additionally, sweetened condensed milk is utilised in the preparation of desserts like cakes, ice creams, and biscuits. It's important to note that vegetable oil-based sweetened creamer is a non-dairy product and does not contain milk solids. Evaporated milk Evaporated milk or unsweetened condensed

--- Chunk 193 ---
Cereal grains, or simply known as cereals, are the edible portion of seeds from the grass family Gramineae. Cereals including rice, corn and wheat are the world’s major food crops which supply more than 60 percent of the global food energy intake (FAO, 1995). Other cereal grains are oats, rye, barley, millet, sorghum and triticale. Although not from the Gramineae family, grains such as buckwheat, amaranth and quinoa are largely similar in nutrition content and preparation methods to the ‘true’ cereals (Grains and Legumes Nutrition Council, 2015). They are therefore considered as cereals in this dietary guideline.

Vegan diets exclude meat, poultry, ﬁsh, seafood, eggs and dairy products and foods that contain these products.

Lacto-vegetarian diets exclude meat, poultry, ﬁsh, seafood and eggs, as well as foods that contain them. Dairy products such as milk, cheese, yogurt and butter are included in the diet.

Ovo-vegetarian diets exclude meat, poultry, ﬁsh, seafood and dairy products but allow eggs.

Lacto-ovo-vegetarian diets exclude meat, poultry, ﬁsh and seafood but allow dairy products and eggs.

In the bran and germ of whole grains, a high concentration of carotenoids including lutein, zeaxanthin, β-cryptoxanthin, β-carotene and α- carotene can be found (Adom et al., 2005; Okarter & Liu, 2010). Additionally, vitamin E (i.e. tocopherols and tocotrienols) are found exclusively in the germ fraction of the whole grains. Speciﬁcally, corn kernel are rich in vitamins A, B1, B2, B3, B5, B6, B9, E, and K, but are less abundant of vitamins B12, C, and D (Acosta-Estrada et al., 2019). In addition, the highest concentration of mineral and phenolic compounds can be found at pericarp germ, and aleurone layer of corn (Serna-Saldivar, 2016).

Protective effects of whole grains on CVD are reported due to various mechanisms (Drewnowski et al., 2021; Seal et al., 2021). Whole grains contain a rich amount of vitamin E, in particular, tocotrienol and ß-sitosterol, which act as antioxidants (Slavin et al., 1999). In addition, the unsaturated fatty acids, mainly oleic and linoleic acid in whole grains help to reduce cholesterol levels (Jonnalagadda et al., 2011).

Healthy diet A healthy diet is a diet that provides a proper combination of energy and nutrients. The four characteristics of a healthy diet are varied, adequate, balanced and moderate.

Legumes Legumes are plants in the Leguminosae family. Legumes comprise pulses and lentils. The terms pulses and lentils are often used interchangeably. Most legumes have nitrogen-ﬁxing bacteria in their root nodules. Peanuts, also known as groundnuts and monkey nuts are legumes despite being called nuts. Example: dhal, tempeh and tauhu.

Malaysian Healthy Plate Malaysian Healthy Plate (Ministry of Health, 2016) is a visual guide to show the total food in each food group that needs to be consumed in a meal to achieve a healthy and balanced diet based on the principle of quarter, quarter, half. Hence, the Malaysian Dietary Guidelines for Vegetarians were created as a useful tool for delivering nutrition advice and guidance based on a realistic and comprehensible scientiﬁc viewpoint. The MDGV comprises 7 Key Messages (KM), prepared by the appointed experts according to each KM, under the coordination of Technical Working Group for Nutritional Guidelines (TWG for Nutritional Guidelines). --- Chunk 223 ---
1.2 Introduction

A healthy diet is vital as the source of energy, nutrients and other food components to maintain health, reduce the risk of diseases and in the management of certain diseases. Eating a balanced and healthy diet can help to prevent nutrient deﬁciencies and excesses such as preventing the excessive weight gain and the risk of chronic diseases such as dyslipidaemia and hypertension (Melina et al., 2016). The Malaysian Dietary Guidelines for Children and Adolescents (NCCFN, 2013) and the Malaysian Dietary Guidelines 2020 (NCCFN, 2021) were the primary references for preparing this guideline. Important considerations were adopted in healthy meal planning, including eating a balanced diet and consuming a wide variety of foods in moderation.

--- Chunk 224 ---
4.3 Scientiﬁc Basis

Vegetarians substitute “meat, poultry or ﬁsh” with various types of eggs, legumes and nuts. The key nutritional is whether substitutions with foods that are appropriate and acceptable to vegetarians, can provide the required nutrients (Philips, 2005). Some nutrients, particularly protein may be difficult to be directly obtained from a vegan diet (Clarys et al., 2014) or vegetarian diets with food allergies. While, there is no published national food allergy prevalence data among Malaysian population, including vegetarians, previous local studies reported that the most common food allergens among atopic children were seafood such as crab, prawn and squid (Zahedi et al., 2011), eggs and cow’s milk (Yadav & Naidu, 2015). It should be noted that childhood food allergies to eggs, milk, wheat and soya typically resolve during childhood, whereas allergies to nuts are persistent (Sicherer & Sampson, 2014). Since vegetarians with food allergy problem have limited choices of food,

--- Chunk 227 ---
Based on the Recommended Nutrient Intake (RNI) for Malaysia (National Coordinating Committee on Food and Nutrition, 2017), a child aged between 1 and 3 years old requires 700 mg of calcium daily and 4 to 9 years old need 1,000 mg/day. During adolescence, the recommended intake increases to 1,300 mg/day. In general, both men and women, including pregnant and lactating women, require 1,000 mg of calcium daily. However, for women above 51 years of age, the recommended intake rises to 1,200 mg/day. Teenagers who are pregnant or lactating are advised to have a higher calcium intake of 1,300 mg/day. By consuming appropriate servings of milk and milk products suitable for their age group, individuals can ensure they meet the recommended calcium intake throughout their lifespan.

6.4 Current Status

Vegetarian diets are in general lower in total fat, SFA, and cholesterol than are non-vegetarian diets. With respect to EFAs intake and balance, vegetarian diets appear to offer no advantages over omnivorous dietary patterns. Vegetarian, especially vegan diets are relatively low in ALA compared with linoleic acid (LA) and provide little, if any, EPA and DHA (Burns-Whitmore, 2019). In view of these ﬁndings, guidance needs to be given to vegetarians in obtaining the appropriate amounts and types of fat in their diet.

1.4 Current Status

There is a lack of data on the dietary patterns of vegetarians in Malaysia. In addition to Cheah et al. (2018)’s study among vegetarians in Sarawak, several unpublished local studies have previously examined the dietary intake of vegetarians, primarily among Buddhists, including monks (Wong, 1999), nuns (Chen, 2001), Chinese adults (Lee, 2000), adolescents (Chong, 2013) and Indians adults (MOH, 2014b). Collectively, these studies' ﬁndings suggest no signiﬁcant differences in nutrient adequacy between vegetarian practices, such as lacto- vegetarians, lacto-ovo-vegetarians and vegans.

--- Chunk 238 ---
However, vegans are prone to calcium deﬁciency, especially during the rapid growth phase in children (Weaver & Plawecki, 1994) and overall bone health (Tucker, 2014). Vegans have reduced bone mineral density, increased incidence of fracture and other health risks compared with omnivores or lacto- vegetarians (Weaver, 2009; Tucker, 2014). Even though intake of minerals, calcium, iron and zinc is related to diet planning, the dietary intake of calcium was noted to be signiﬁcantly higher among vegetarians as compared with non-vegetarians in a study in Kuala Lumpur (Wong, 2013). Careful meal planning, calcium-fortiﬁed foods or drinks are essential together with evaluation on the need for (Weaver & supplementation among vegans Plawecki, 1994).

A food pyramid acts as a visual guide to provide a framework for the types and amounts of foods that can be eaten in combination to provide a nutritious and healthy daily diet. The levels in the food pyramid from the bottom to the top indicate that a person should eat more of the foods at the base and fewer foods intake from the top of the pyramid. Similarly, the Malaysian Food Pyramid for Vegetarians (Figure 1.2) is a practical visual guide for vegetarians to choose and eat a variety of foods of their choice. This pyramid was modelled after the Malaysian Food Pyramid with the meat sources removed (NCCFN, 2021).

The principles of the vegetarian pyramid are similar to the general population food pyramid, with some modiﬁcations requirements of vegetarian individuals. The recommended number of servings indicates an average amount that individuals should choose to eat each day, and it

Rice has the highest digestibility among the staples, due to its low dietary ﬁbre and tannin content (FAO,

On the contrary, foods that are minimally processed such as whole grains and their products usually have low GI/ GL properties. These foods have slower rates of digestion and absorption, hence reducing the rapid elevation of postprandial hyperglycemia, as well as insulin concentration (Yusof et al., 2009). Whole grains may be eaten whole, cracked, split, ﬂaked or ground. Most often, they are milled into ﬂour and used to make breads, cereals, pasta, crackers and other cereal-based foods.

Fruits juice contains high amount of sugar, without any ﬁbre which would provide chewing resistance, thus limiting intake. According to Gill and Satter (2014), “fruits juice contains just as much sugar and calories as a sugary carbonated drink and sometimes even more”. For instance, 250 ml of apple juice typically contains 110 kcal and 26 g of sugar, which is similar to the energy and sugar content of sugar-sweetened soda such as 250 ml of cola that typically contains 105 kcal and 26.5 g of sugar (Gill et al., 2014). It is therefore easy to consume a large amount of calories from fruits juices without getting any actual nutrition. In addition, it is also found that 100% fruits juices have low levels of antioxidants compared to whole oranges and other plant-based foods such as vegetables (Crowe & Murray, 2013). --- Chunk 265 ---
Malaysian Food Pyramid for Vegetarians A food pyramid is a visual tool used as a guide to your daily food intake in order to achieve a recommended servings of food groups in the diet. It provides a useful guide based on types and amounts of food to be eaten in combination to achieve a balanced and healthy diet. A food pyramid consists of four different levels, represented by main ﬁve food groups. This indicates that an individual should eat more of the foods at the base of the pyramid and less of the foods at the top of the pyramid. The Malaysian Food Pyramid for Vegetarians is modiﬁed from the Malaysian Food Pyramid 2020, that animal sources were removed. The recommended food servings in this food pyramid is used for children aged 7 years and older, adolescents and adults, and it can be practiced by vegetarians such lacto-, lacto-ovo-, ovo- and vegan).

--- Chunk 268 ---
3.3.5.4Whole grains and body weight management

In a systematic review of observational studies, high (approximately three intake of whole grains servings/day) has been associated with lower BMI and waist circumference compared to those with low whole grain intake (<0.5 servings/day) (Harland & Garton, 2008). This ﬁnding was supported by another two recent systematic reviews and meta- analysis where whole grain intake was associated with lower body weight (Maki et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020).

--- Chunk 269 ---
Global practice of vegetarianism

A plant-based or vegetarian diet revolves around consuming predominantly plant-derived foods, including whole grains, legumes, beans, nuts, seeds, oils, fruits, and vegetables. Notably, numerous inﬂuential historical ﬁgures, such as Pythagoras, Plato, George Bernard Shaw, Mahatma Gandhi, Albert Einstein, Leonardo da Vinci, and Leo Tolstoy, have embraced vegetarianism (Leitzmann, 2014). The practice of vegetarianism takes on various forms worldwide (Fehér et al., 2020), exhibiting regional and cultural variations. India has one of the highest rates of vegetarianism, while Israel, Italy, Germany, Taiwan, and certain European nations have notably high rates of vegetarianism. In North America, the percentage is 6 percent, while in Europe, it is 5 percent (Memon et al., 2021). Approximately 16 percent of individuals in Africa and the Middle East, and 8 percent in Central and South America, are vegetarians.

food

7.3 Current Status

Studies on the usage of food labels were mainly conducted among consumers without any dietary restrictions. A nationwide cohort of 42,750 Thai adults found that 89.0% read food labels, of which 64.4% were frequent users (Rimpeekool et al., 2017). A cross-sectional study on Filipino adults conducted by Sy and Bullecer (2020) found that 87.7% read nutrition labels when they purchased a food product. In Israel, 59.3% of adults aged 21 and above reported that the information on food labels

often or always affects their decision to purchase a food product (Shahrabani, 2021). In Malaysia, the Malaysian Adult Nutrition Survey reported that 45% of adults read food labels (Ambak et al., 2018). Another local study conducted by Norazlanshah et al. (2013) on 165 university students in Kuantan reported that 57.6% read the food labels before purchasing a food product. However, there are no studies on food labels among vegetarians.

Unsaturated fatty acids There are two types of unsaturated fatty acids, namely monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFA) and polyunsaturated (PUFA). The predominant MUFA in the diet is oleic acid (C18:1) whilst the PUFA consists of two groups, the omega- 3 fatty acid [e.g., alpha-linolenic acid (ALA, C18:3), eicosapentaenoic and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA, C22:6)] and the omega-6 fatty acid [e.g., linoleic acid (LA, C18:2) and arachidonic acid (AA, C20:4)]. LA and ALA are known as essential fatty acids (EFA) as they cannot be synthesised by humans and therefore must be included in the diet.

Zinc is second only to iron among trace elements in the body. Zinc deﬁciency is related to poor bioavailability of zinc from vegetarian diets (Hunt, 2003). Dietary zinc intakes and serum zinc concentrations were lower in habitual vegetarian adults compared with non-vegetarian counterparts (Foster, Chu, Petocz, & Samman, 2013; Gorczyca et al., 2013). However, in older adults, children, and women during pregnancy and lactation, there is insufficient evidence to determine whether zinc intake and status are lower in vegetarians compared to omnivores (Foster & Samman, 2015). A meta- analysis reported that dietary zinc intake was lower in pregnant vegetarians when compared to non- vegetarians and both groups consumed lower than recommended amounts (Foster et al., 2015).

Eggs are excellent source of protein for ovo- vegetarians. They are also suitable for many types of cooking methods. One chicken egg contains about 6 g of protein. Approximately 12.6% of the weight of the chicken egg is protein and this can be found in both the yolk and albumen (Laymen & Rodriquez, 2009). It is also a rich source of leucine, which is lacking in wheat. Eggs are also good source of vitamin B12, riboﬂavin (vitamin B2), retinol (vitamin A), vitamin D, vitamin E, folate, iodine, selenium, phosphorus, zinc and haem iron (Miranda et al., 2015; Réhault-Godbert & Guyot, 2019). Approximately 9% of the weight of the chicken egg is fat, which is found almost entirely in the yolk. The fatty acid proﬁle is 38% mono-unsaturated fatty acids, 16% polyunsaturated fatty acids and 28% saturated fatty acids. Eggs produced by chicken fed on ﬂaxseed contain long chain omega-3 fatty acids

Nonetheless, whole grains intake does not affect body weight and obesity measures in a systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Sadeghi et al., 2020). The mechanism might explain the inverse association between whole grain and weight gain.

6.2 Introduction

Fats supply energy and essential fatty acids and serve as a carrier for the absorption of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K and carotenoids. Fats serve as building blocks of membranes and play a key regulatory role in numerous biological functions such as maintaining a regular heartbeat, providing an regulating cholesterol and contributing to brain and eye development in developing babies. The optimum amount of fat in our diet depends on our stage of life. The recommended total fat intake is between 25% and 30% of calories for both vegetarian and non- vegetarian adults (NCCFN, 2017).

Tubers such as potatoes, sweet potatoes, cassava and yam cultivate well in diverse soils and environments, including conditions which are not suitable for cereal production. Traditionally, tubers are widely grown and consumed as subsistence staples in humid and sub-humid tropics, such as Asia, Paciﬁc Islands, Africa and Latin American (FAO, 1998). Tubers have a higher moisture content ranging from 60- 90% compared to 10-15% moisture content in cereal grains. Due to higher moisture content, tubers have lower energy- and nutrient densities relative to cereals (FAO, 1993).

Key Message 6Include appropriate amounts and types of fat in the diet6.1 Terminology Cholesterol Cholesterol is a waxy, fat-like substance found in all animals including people. Cholesterol is an essential part of cells in the body and is used to make certain hormones and digest fats. The primary source of cholesterol in the body is the liver (blood or serum cholesterol), while dietary cholesterol which comes from foods of animal origin provides a much smaller amount by comparison (Whitney & Sharon, 2005). Essential fatty acids Essential fatty acids (EFAs) refer to the polyunsaturated omega-6 fatty acid, linoleic acid (C18:2) and the polyunsaturated omega-3 fatty acid, alpha-linolenic acid (C18:3). These fatty acids cannot be synthesised by the human body and must therefore be provided by the diet. “Omega” in fatty acid nomenclature refers to the position of the ﬁrst carbon-carbon double bond counting from the methyl (CH3) end of the molecule (Vaclavik & Christian, 2014). 7.2.4 Hypersensitivity listing

Consumers with food allergies need to have clear information about the ingredients used in the foods they buy to successfully avoid the foods that they know they are sensitive to. While numerous foods have been identiﬁed as sources of allergic reactions, 90% of the allergic reactions associated with foods are caused by one of these eight foods: milk, eggs, ﬁsh, crustacean shellﬁsh, peanuts, tree nuts, wheat and soy (Anderson et al., 2010).

The Malaysian Food Regulations 1985 requires food industries to disclose any of the top ﬁve foods or food groups that may cause hypersensitivity as below:

1. Cereal containing gluten including wheat, rye, barley and oat

2. Nut and nut products, including peanut and soya bean

3. Fish and ﬁsh products 4. Milk and milk products (including lactose) 5. Egg and egg products

--- Chunk 322 ---
The main way to overcome the incomplete amino acid proﬁle in plant proteins is through eating a mixture of plant protein foods (Bressani, 1988). To achieve true protein complementation effect, two plant protein foods, each of which supplies the amino acids missing in the other, are consumed together. For example, cereals are paired with legumes and nuts which lack methionine but are rich in lysine. Consumption of mixed foods with complementary proteins can provide a well- balanced protein source (Friedman, 1996). Therefore, when consumed in appropriate amounts and in combination with nuts and legumes at different meals over the course of the day, cereals and tubers can contribute towards complete proteins in a vegetarian diet (Mariotti & Gardner, 2019; Melina et al., 2016).

--- Chunk 339 ---
Structurally, each seed of a cereal grain has a protective outer husk, a bran covering, a starchy endosperm and a germ. Because rough husks or chaff of grains are not usually consumed by humans, they are removed to produce whole grains that consist of the bran, germ and endosperm (Figure 3.1). Therefore, whole grains are intact, ground, cracked or ﬂacked kernels after removal of the inedible husks (van der Kamp et al., 2014). Among common types of whole grains are unpolished rice (brown), whole wheat, de-hulled barley, oats, corn, rye, millet and buckwheat.

3.3.5.3Whole grains and reduced risk of cancer

review of meta-analyses of A systematic observational studies reported that whole grain intake was associated with total cancer mortality, where daily intake of 15 g to 90 g of whole grain resulted in 3% to 20% reduction in the risk (Gaesser, 2020). For site-speciﬁc cancers, whole grain intake was associated with colorectal, colon, gastric, pancreatic and esophageal cancers (Gaesser, 2020). This ﬁnding was supported by another systematic review and meta-analysis (Zhang et al., 2020). Whole grain consumption may offer protection for colorectal cancer by increasing stool bulk, diluting faecal carcinogens, decreasing transit time and production of short chain fatty acids through colonic fermentation.

--- Chunk 354 ---
Protein levels of cereals and tubers range widely; from 1- 2 g per 100 g in tubers to 7-14 g per 100 g in cereals (FAO, 1993). For instance, after cooking, every 150 g of rice and potatoes contain approximately 3.5 g and 2.5 g of protein, respectively (Tee et al., 1997). Similar to legumes, nuts, seeds and vegetables, the concentrations of protein are lower in cereals and tubers compared to animal foods (Young & Pellett, 1994). Therefore, it is not surprising that typical vegetarians have lower protein intake compared to meat-eaters (Cade et al., 2004; Clarys et al., 2014; Gan et al., 2018). Nevertheless, cereals and tubers are important sources of proteins in a vegetarian diet, particularly for vegans who omit milk and eggs in their diets. Cereals and legumes can provide 11% of plant proteins (75% of total protein) in semi- vegetarian diets and up to 13.5% (96% of total protein) in strict vegetarian diets (Rizzo et al., 2013).

6.3.5 Essential fatty acids

The sources of omega-3 fatty acids include ALA and marine-derived acids omega-3 eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA). ALA, the starter EFAs, generates an even longer chain EPA and DHA (omega-3) while linoleic acid generates arachidonic acid (AA) (omega-6). EPA is the precursor of the series 3 eicosanoids which oppose the negative effects (vasoconstriction, fever, pain and inﬂammation) of the series 2 eicosanoids derived from AA (Calder, 2012; Harris, 2014). These EFAs are the omega-6 linoleic acid (LA) and the omega-3 alpha linolenic acid (ALA), which are required for cell membrane structure and function and for the synthesis of “local hormones” called eicosanoids (Tony Ng et al., 2019). Thus, EPA-derived eicosanoids are ‘good’ while those derived from AA are ‘bad’.

While the prevalence of vegetarianism among Malaysians remains uncertain, there is a noticeable increase in its adoption due to concerns surrounding health, religion, the environment, animal welfare, ethics, and food sustainability. 6.3 Scientiﬁc Basis

Fats and oils are an essential part of a diet, however the type and total amount of fat consumed makes a difference to health. High intake of saturated fats and cholesterol increases the risk of unhealthy blood lipid levels, which, in turn, may increase the risk of coronary heart disease (CHD). Whereas, a low intake of fats and oils increases the risk of inadequate intakes of vitamin E and essential fatty acids and

may contribute to unfavourable changes in high- density lipoprotein (HDL) blood cholesterol and triglycerides. Compared to non-vegetarian diets, vegetarian diets tend to be lower in total fat, saturated fat, monounsaturated fat, cholesterol and α-linolenic acid (ALA) (an omega-3 fatty acid) (Rizzo et al., 2013; Wong et al., 2013; Elorinne et al., 2016; Gan et al., 2018; Ching, Y.K, Chin et al., 2019).

6.3.4 Trans fatty acids

To date, there are only limited number of evidence have suggested that vegetarians or vegans had a lower intake of trans fatty acids (TFA) compared to those of non-vegetarians (Lee et al., 2000; Rizzo et al., 2013; Chamorro et al., 2020). For instance, a study found that vegetarians had a markedly lower serum TFA level than non-vegetarians (0.03% compared with 0.50% of total TFA, respectively) (Lee et al., 2000). A greater level of TFA in non-vegetarians was mainly due to the frequent consumption of TFA- containing food including commercial baked goods, shortening, microwave popcorn, frozen pizza and stick margarine (Lee et al., 2000).

foods, particularly processed

omnivorous

Limited local evidence suggests a positive association between higher diet quality and anthropometry and clinical outcomes (Ramadas et al., 2021). Higher diet quality has also been consistently associated with a lower risk of all-cause mortality, especially cardiovascular disease (CVD), type 2 diabetes and cancer (Miller et al., 2020; Morze et al., 2020). 7.2.6 Food labelling issue faced by vegetarians

The main purpose of food labelling is to assist consumers in making appropriate food choices; however, the current system does not allow vegetarians to have full access to the information they need to make these decisions. Vegetarians found it difficult to identify foods that suited their lifestyles. Vegetarians have to read food labels to avoid animal products. When they have queries about speciﬁc food products, they must directly contact the manufacturer. Misleading labels or lack of listing all ingredients makes vegetarians more susceptible to unconsciously breaking the rules of not consuming foods of animal origin. Some issues that vegetarians usually face include using “natural ingredients”, whereby the food might be plant or animal-based sources such as lecithin (Fields, 2011).

--- Chunk 385 ---
Vitamin B12 plays a crucial role in red blood cell production and the prevention of anaemia. As plant- based foods do not naturally contain vitamin B12, it is important for individuals following a vegetarian diet to incorporate alternative sources or fortiﬁed foods to meet the recommended intake. Vegans, in particular, are recommended to include vitamin supplements, vitamin-enriched cereals, and fortiﬁed products in their diet. For example, fortiﬁed plant- based milk, breakfast cereals, and nutritional yeast are common sources of vitamin B12 for vegans.

--- Chunk 386 ---
Research shows generally there is low milk consumption among Malaysians, in both adults and children. According to the ﬁndings from the Malaysian Adult Nutrition Survey (MANS) in 2014, Malaysian adults were only consumed about 1.4 servings of milk and/or dairy products in a day, either fresh or commercially-based milk products, the which was at recommended intake of 1-3 servings per day (Institute for Public Health, 2014; Lee & Wan Muda, 2019). Malaysians tend to neglect the importance of milk as they grow older and opt for sugar-sweetened beverages such as tea, coffee and cordials. Almost, 59% of Malaysians drink sugar and sweetened condensed milk daily. Women were shown to be frequent drinkers of full cream milk compared to men who preferred sweetened condensed milk. Urban populations were drinking more full cream milk and the rural population preferred sweetened condensed milk (Norimah et al., 2008).

Compelling evidence from epidemiological and experimental studies indicates that diets rich in vegetables and fruits exert signiﬁcant beneﬁcial effects on general health and wellbeing, and lower the risk of non-communicable diseases such as cardiovascular diseases, type-II diabetes and certain types of cancers (Dauchet et al., 2009; Boeing et al., 2012; Slavin & Lloyd, 2012; Zhu et al., 2018; Wallace et al., 2020). Hence, vegetables and fruits are clearly an important part of a healthy diet meal in vegetarians of all types. It should be noted that consumption of a variety of vegetables and fruits is as important as the quantity, because no single fruits or vegetable provides all essential nutrients. Therefore, regardless of types of vegetarian practices, consuming adequate amounts of a variety of different vegetables and fruits each day is highly recommended to ensure an adequate intake of ﬁbre, vitamins, minerals and a multitude of other important bioactive compounds.

The primary objective of a food label on pre- packaged food is to inform consumers about the product’s characteristics at the point of purchase. The label provides information that describes what is contained in a package to guide consumers in making appropriate choices. The main information on a food label includes the appropriate name of the product. These ingredients are used to prepare the food, food additives used, net weight or volume, expiry date and name, and address of the manufacturer. Where appropriate, food labels also provide information on food hypersensitivity in a product. Some food labels also state which country the product originated from.

There are no speciﬁc labelling requirements for vegetarian foods in Malaysia. Nevertheless, as mentioned above, most of the information required to be on the food label is relevant and useful in helping vegetarians choose appropriate products. This is particularly relevant when vegetarians avoid certain food groups or ingredients.

Although total iron intake in a national sample of British children aged 4 years old to 18 years old were not signiﬁcantly different between vegetarians and non-vegetarians, vegetarian adolescent girls were more likely to have poorer iron status than their meat-eating counterparts (Thane, Bates, & Prentice, 2003). Several human studies have shown an inverse association between fruits and vegetable intake and blood pressure (Miura et al., 2004; Dauchet et al., 2007). 2.3.3 Gastrointestinal health

Dietary ﬁbre is an important nutrient which determines the overall gastrointestinal health status (Anderson et al., 2009). Adequate intake of ﬁbre is important to ensure the normal function of the digestive system. Numerous studies conducted in children and adults have shown that a low intake of ﬁbre is associated with an increased risk of constipation (Dukas et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2008). A follow-up study of 3327 adult women aged 36 to 61 years found that a high intake of daily ﬁbre of approximately 20 g per day reduced the risk of constipation by 3-fold compared to those having a daily intake of 7 g of ﬁbre (Dukas et al., 2003). Hence, a simple and easy strategy to increase dietary ﬁbre intake could be to increase the consumption of a variety of vegetables and fruits each day.

--- Chunk 419 ---
Evidence from prospective cohort studies and secondary prevention trials suggest that omega-3 and omega-6 should be consumed in appropriate proportions for one’s cardiovascular health. Any imbalances between these fatty acids can cancel out the beneﬁts of omega-3 fatty acids (Shahidi & Ambigaipalan, 2018). Excessive amounts of omega- 6 PUFAs and a very high omega-6/omega-3 PUFAs ratio, found in typical Western diets, promote the development of CVD, cancer, inﬂammatory and autoimmune diseases; whereas increased levels of omega-3 PUFAs (lower omega-6/omega-3 ratio), exert beneﬁcial effects. A ratio of 2-5/1 (omega- 6/omega-3 PUFAs) is recommended. A lower ratio of omega-6/omega-3 PUFAs is more desirable in reducing the risk of many chronic diseases (Shahidi & Ambigaipalan, 2018). A typical diet which provides proportionately high amounts of unsaturated fats with balanced omega-6/omega-3 PUFAs ratio is the Mediterranean diet, commonly consumed by people in Italy, Spain, Portugal, Greece, Croatia and Cyprus. It

--- Chunk 420 ---
Greater intakes of TFA were linked to CHD risk in many epidemiological studies including the Nurses’ Health Study (Curtis et al., 2016), The Zutphen study (Oomen et al., 2001), the Health Professionals Follow-up study (Mozaffarian et al., 2006), the Alpha- Tocopherol Beta-Carotene Trial (Simila et al., 2013) as well as in a review of prospective observational studies (Teegala et al., 2009). A 23% overall increased risk of CHD for each additional 2% energy intake from a total of TFA was reported when all other available evidence were combined (Mozaffarian et al., 2006).

Due the adverse health effects, WHO recommends less than 1% of TFA consumption of total energy intakes (WHO, 2018). However, the levels of TFAs in Malaysian foods are somewhat low. This is because most Malaysian food items are produced using palm oil rather than hydrogenated PUFA which are commonly used abroad (Filippou et al., 2014). Currently, TFA labelling is not mandatory in Malaysia.

Concerns regarding the ability of vegetarian diets to meet protein needs are primarily based on the quality of protein consumed, which is determined by amino acid content and digestibility (Mangels, Messina, & Messina, 2011; Mariotti & Gardner,

2019). Protein of animal origins are considered as high quality because they provide all the essential amino acids adequately, while plant or vegetable proteins are not of the same quality because of low content of some essential amino acids. Nevertheless, a combination of cereals, millets and legumes provides most of the amino acids that complement each other to provide adequate essential amino acids. A healthy vegetarian diet can meet all the body nutrient needs at any stage of life including pregnancy, lactation and for older adults.

Saturated fatty acids Saturated fatty acids (SFAs) from dietary fats and oils do not carry any carbon-carbon double bonds in the fatty acid chain. SFAs common to the human diet have 12 to 18 carbons, namely lauric acid (C12:0), myristic acid (C14:0), palmitic acid (C16:0) and stearic acid (C18:0). SFAs of 12 to 16 carbons are known to raise blood cholesterol levels, whilst stearic acid and SFAs less than 12 carbons are considered neutral. Saturated fat is found in signiﬁcant amounts in animal foods, such as the visible fat on meat and chicken, butter, cream and full fat dairy products, and in plant foods like coconut oil (DeBruyne et al., 2012; Vaclavik & Christian, 2014).

Skimmed/non-fat milk Skimmed/ non-fat milk is milk from which milk fat has been removed but with most of the other essential nutrients intact. It is useful for those who want to limit their intake of energy, fat and cholesterol.

Ultra-high temperature (UHT) milk Ultra-high temperature (UHT) milk is milk which has been subjected to heat treatment by being retained at a temperature of not less than 135oC for at least two seconds to render it commercially sterile and immediately aseptically packed in sterile containers.

Milk product Milk product is the term used to describe milk- based or milk-related products such as cheese, butter, ghee (clariﬁed butter oil), yogurt, keﬁr and ice cream (Food Regulations, 1985). It is usually milk or a product thereof, whether alone or combined with another agricultural product, that contains no oil or fat other than that of milk (Food Regulations, 1985).

Sterilised milk Sterilised milk is milk which has been ﬁltered, homogenised and heated to a temperature of not less than 100°C and maintained at the temperature for length to a time sufficient.

Milk Milk refers to a white liquid in raw or fresh form produced by the mammary glands of animals such as cows, buffalo, goats and sheep. Milk is a complex mixture of lipids, carbohydrates, proteins and many other organic, as well as inorganic compounds. Milk should consist of at least 3.25% milk fat and 8.50% of non-fat milk solids. Plant foods such as legumes and nuts are important dietary sources of zinc, yet, are also high in phytic acid, an inhibitor of zinc bioavailability (Saunders, Craig & Baines, 2013). Zinc absorption is reduced when consuming plant foods that are high in phytates, while zinc absorption is enhanced when consuming animal protein. Legumes and nuts, although not as good as animal protein, can enhance the zinc absorption among vegetarians. The European Food Safety Authority assumes a bioavailability of 20% for zinc if the diet is predominantly vegetarian (EFSA NDA Panel, 2014). Zinc deﬁciency can cause poor growth and delayed sex maturation in children, hair loss, poor wound healing, loss of appetite, skin rashes and impaired immune function.

It is crucial to include all food groups in the daily diet, considering the nutritional values of each of food groups. Insufficient or excessive intake of these foods should be avoided as both situations have signiﬁcant implications on an individual’s health. Balanced vegetarian diets meet the nutritional needs of all life cycle stages, including pregnancy, lactation, infancy, childhood, adolescence and the elderly (Melina et al., 2016). Well-planned vegetarians tend to consume fewer overall calories; a lower proportion of calories from fat (particularly saturated fat) and cholesterol; and higher intakes of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, nuts, soy products, ﬁbre and phytochemicals than non-vegetarians. Because of the variability in vegetarian diets, individuals need to become familiar with their individual nutritional needs and potential dietary deﬁciencies.

SFAs have harmful effects on health such as weight gain, which is associated with diabetes, and raising blood cholesterol levels. A pooled analysis of 13 epidemiologic studies showed a signiﬁcant relationship between dietary SFA intake and increased risk of coronary events and coronary mortality in middle-aged and older men and women (Micha & Mozaffarian, 2010). It is thus advisable to limit SFA consumption to not greater than 10% of total calories to prevent the risk of raising blood cholesterol level. A meta-analyses of prospective cohort studies reported pooled relative risk estimates comparing extremes of intake of SFA of 1.07 (95% conﬁdence interval 0.96 to 1.19; P=0.22) for CHD, 0.81 (0.62 to 1.05; P=0.11) for stroke and 1.00 (0.89 to 1.11; P=0.95) for cardiovascular diseases (CVD) 2010). Adequate calcium intake can be achieved in both vegetarians and non-vegetarians through careful diet planning (Yen et al., 2008; Mangels, 2014). For instance, diets rich in fruits and vegetables have positively been associated with positive calcium balance, as assessed by numerous bone metabolism markers in men and women (Calvez et al., 2012; Brondani et al., 2019). This can be attributed to the high potassium and magnesium content in fruits and vegetables, which produce an alkaline ash that helps inhibit bone resorption and reduce calcium loss through urine (Higgs et al., 2017). Additionally, engaging in regular exercise is beneﬁcial as it helps reduce calcium loss from bones, further supporting overall bone health.

--- Chunk 460 ---
Iodine is a component in thyroid hormones that help to regulate the metabolism, growth and function of key organs. Vegans may not get enough iodine and be at risk of deﬁciency and possibly, goitre. Soya beans, cruciferous vegetables and sweet potatoes may contain goitrogens, substances that can promote goiter formation. However, incorporating these foods in moderation and focusing on non-goitrogenic options can help vegans meet their iodine requirements. Non- goitrogenic foods rich in iodine include seaweed, kelp, pumpkin, tomato, bell peppers, green beans, peas, cucumber, asparagus, eggplant, carrots, and celery. Some non-goitrogenic fruits vegans should eat include mangoes, citrus fruits, blueberries, dark- skinned grapes, pomegranates, guavas, cherries, apricots, apples, pineapples and kiwis. The use of iodised salt as much as 1/4 teaspoon a day can provide a signiﬁcant amount of iodine.

Protein is needed for growth and maintenance of body tissues. It is also necessary for enzymes, hormones, antibodies and for milk production in women who are breastfeeding. Amino acids are building blocks of proteins. Proteins consist of combination of 20 unique amino acids. There are nine essential amino acids that have to be obtained through dietary sources, as these nutrients cannot be synthesized in our body. The remaining eleven amino acids that can be synthesized in our body are nutritionally non-essential (Table 4.1). In a non- vegetarian diet, proteins are obtained from animal sources and plant sources. Animal sources such as eggs, meat and ﬁsh provide all essential amino acids required by the body in the correct ratio. Lysine, methionine, cystine, threonine, tryptophan and leucine are essential amino acids because the human body requires them but is unable to synthesize them. In healthy adult humans, the estimated requirement of amino acids is lysine 50 mg/g protein, methionine and cysteine 25 mg/g

Salt and sugar are both ﬂavour enhancers in foods and/ or beverages. Besides being ﬂavour-enhancing agents, salt and sugar provide some health and nutrition beneﬁts. However, excessive salt and sugar consumption in foods and beverages has been linked to chronic non-communicable diseases. For example, high intakes of salt/ sodium have been strongly linked to hypertension (WHO, 2012) and stomach cancer (D'Elia et al., 2012), while high sugar intake has been associated with overweight and in children. obesity, Therefore, it is vital to limit salt and the use and intake of salt and sugar in a vegetarian diet. With that, vegetarians are recommended to apply the key messages and related key recommendations on salt and sugar, which are available in the Malaysian Dietary Guidelines.

Types of vegetarian diets

Ovo-vegetarian: Ovo-vegetarians exclude meat, ﬁsh, poultry, and dairy products from their diet but include eggs.

Vegan: Vegans follow a strict plant-based diet and avoid all animal products, including meat, ﬁsh, poultry, dairy, eggs, and honey. They rely solely on plant-based foods for their nutrition.

In addition to the common types of vegetarians, there are a few other types of vegetarian diets, such as:

Pescatarian: Pescatarians follow a primarily vegetarian diet but include ﬁsh and other seafood in their meals. They abstain from consuming meat and poultry but include plant-based foods, dairy products, eggs, and seafood.

7.2.5 Nutrition information on food labels

Although not speciﬁcally for vegetarians, nutrition information on food labels is also useful in making appropriate food choices. These include nutrients declared in the nutrition information panel (NIP) and nutrition claims. It also includes front-of-pack nutrition labelling (FOP-NL) which comprises energy icon and healthier choice logo (Refer to Key Message 14 of the Malaysian Dietary Guidelines 2020). Vegetarians should effectively use such information on food labels to understand the energy and content of nutrients.

The biological importance of omega-6 fatty acids relates to growth (Semba et al., 2017), fertility and strengthening of skin and red blood cell structure, whereas omega-3 fatty acids are important for cell structure and function of the retina and nervous system. All these connect to the human body’s speciﬁc requirement for linoleic acid or ALA, and hence regarded as EFAs (Harris, 2014).

Vanaspati Vanaspati is a vegetable substitute for ghee and is produced by hydrogenation of vegetable oils such as soya bean, sunﬂower, cottonseed, canola and palm oil. It is mainly produced in India, Iran, Pakistan and some other Arabic and African countries. Other names of vanaspati include vegetable ghee, culinary hydrogenated vegetable oil and grainy fat (Farmani et al., 2007; Downs et al., 2013). Vanaspati is generally used as an all-purpose culinary fat in frying, baking and cooking applications (Labbe et al., 2009). Vanaspati contains high amounts of TFAs, and are therefore associated with increased risk of coronary heart disease in adults (Farmani & Golitabar, 2015).

Whole grain consumption provides better protection against type 2 diabetes risk than total intake of grains or reﬁned grains. A analysis of dietary intake data from the three largest prospective cohorts have also found that whole grains consumptions lower risk of type 2 diabetes (Hu et al., 2020). Interestingly, most of the risk reduction occurred when whole grain intake was up to two servings per day, suggesting that at least two servings of whole grains should be consumed to reduce type 2 diabetes risk. nature. Minimally processed foods are natural foods altered by methods that include the removal of inedible or unwanted parts, and also processes that include drying, crushing, grinding, powdering, fractioning, ﬁltering, roasting, boiling, non-alcoholic freezing, fermentation, pasteurisation, chilling, placing in containers, and vacuum packaging. Unprocessed and minimally processed foods vary in energy density, their content and balance of fats, carbohydrates, proteins, and their fractions, and vitamins, minerals, and other bioactive compounds (Lane et al., 2021; Monteiro et al., 2019b).

Variety Variety refers to eating many different types of foods each day to ensure a better selection of healthier foods. By selecting a variety of foods, the chances of consuming the multitude of nutrients the body needs are optimised.

Another area of concern is the low biological value of protein in plant-based proteins and the lack of essential amino acids. 7.2.2 Ingredient listing

One of the regulatory requirements of a food label is ingredient listing. Pre-packaged food products must have a list of ingredients on the packaging except for single-ingredient products. Ingredients are listed in descending order of proportions by weight. This means that the ingredients listed earlier in the list are found in greater amounts than those lower in the list.

Ingredient listing is useful to vegetarians. They can scan through the list and avoid products containing animal origin ingredients. Consumers can easily recognise these ingredients, as the law requires that the animal’s common name must be given if the ingredients are of animal origin. In addition, it is also a requirement that if the product contains edible fat or oil, the common name of the animal or vegetable source of the fat or oil must be stated.

There is no data on whole grain consumption patterns of Malaysian adults. A national study on whole grain intakes of Malaysian primary and secondary school children showed that only 25% of children and 19% of adolescents are whole grain consumers. 3.3 Scientiﬁc Basis

The Malaysian Food Pyramid for Vegetarians suggests that vegetarians consume adequate amounts of cereals, cereal-based products and tubers as part of a healthy diet. This food group contains a myriad of nutrients, including carbohydrates, proteins, dietary ﬁbre, vitamins, minerals and phytochemicals, hence contributing to a balanced vegetarian diet. The recommended serving for this food group is from 3 to 7, with cereal products preferably being whole grain. This recommendation is consistent with many international dietary guidelines for the general population, including the Malaysian Food Pyramid (NCCFN, 2021).

and Operations

The goal of the clinician is to match the intensity of preventive efforts with an individual’s absolute risk of a future ASCVD event and with the individual’s willing- ness and capacity to implement preventive strategies. Risk estimation is imperfect and based on group aver- ages that are then applied to individual patients. The clinician must balance an understanding of a patient’s estimated ASCVD risk with potential benefits and ad- verse risk from pharmacological therapy in the context of a risk discussion. To determine the appropriateness of pharmacological therapy after quantitative risk estima- tion in cases that are unclear, risk-enhancing factors or selective use of a coronary artery calcium measurement can inform decision-making for cholesterol-lowering or antihypertensive medication use in intermediate-risk in- dividuals.

--- Chunk 13 ---
Older patients (men 55–80 y of age; women 60–80 y of age) with low burden of risk factorsS4.4-42 who question whether they would benefit from statin therapy

Middle-aged adults (40–55 y of age) with PCE-calculated 10-year risk for ASCVD 5% to <7.5% with factors that increase their ASCVD risk, although they are in a borderline risk group.

Caveats: If patient is at intermediate risk and if a risk decision is uncertain and a coronary artery calcium score is obtained, it is reasonable to withhold statin therapy unless higher-risk conditions, such as cigarette smoking, family history of premature ASCVD, or diabetes mellitus, are present and to reassess the coronary artery calcium score in 5 to 10 years. Moreover, if coronary artery calcium is recommended, it should be performed in facilities that have current technology and expertise to deliver the lowest radiation possible.

--- Chunk 17 ---
1.4. Scope of the Guideline This guideline is intended to be a resource for the clinical and public health practice communities. It addresses the primary prevention of CVD in adults (≥18 years of age), focused on outcomes of ASCVD (ie, acute coronary syndromes, MI, stable or unstable angina, arterial revascularization, stroke, transient ischemic attack, or peripheral arterial disease of ath- erosclerotic origin), as well as heart failure and atrial fibrillation. The guideline presents recommendations to prevent CVD that are related to lifestyle factors (eg, diet and exercise or physical activity), other factors af-

fecting CVD risk (eg, obesity, diabetes, blood choles- terol, high BP, smoking, aspirin use), patient-centered approaches (eg, team-based care, shared decision- making, assessment of social determinants of health), and considerations of the cost and value of primary prevention.

The ACC/AHA Task Force on Clinical Practice Guide- lines has commissioned this guideline to consolidate existing recommendations and various recent scientific statements, expert consensus documents, and clinical practice guidelines into a single guidance document fo- cused on the primary prevention of ASCVD. The integration of value assessments into our na- tional guidelines involves inherent methodological chal- lenges, including: 1) variability in costs across different healthcare settings; 2) variability in costs and benefits across different patient subgroups; 3) variability over time; 4) variability in who bears the burden of the health outcome (ie, typically the individual patient) ver- sus who bears the burden of the healthcare cost (eg, often spread beyond the individual to third-party pay- ers, taxpayers); and 5) an inadequate literature base on which to render a sound, evidence-based assessment of certain specific therapies.S5-1,S5-2

PREAMBLE Since 1980, the American College of Cardiology (ACC) and American Heart Association (AHA) have translated scientific evidence into clinical practice guidelines with recommendations to improve cardiovascular health. These guidelines, which are based on systematic meth- ods to evaluate and classify evidence, provide a founda- tion for the delivery of quality cardiovascular care. The ACC and AHA sponsor the development and publica- tion of clinical practice guidelines without commercial support, and members volunteer their time to the writ- ing and review efforts.

1.1. Methodology and Evidence Review This guideline continues the ACC and AHA effort to de- sign a comprehensive yet succinct compilation of practi- cal guidance for the primary prevention of ASCVD and to promote optimal dissemination of information by us- ing concise language and formatting. The recommen- dations listed in this guideline are evidence based and supported by an extensive evidence review. A search for literature derived from research involving human sub- jects, published in English, and indexed in Ovid MED- LINE, PubMed, Cochrane Library, National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), and other selected databases relevant to this guideline, was conducted be- tween May and July 2018. For specific search terms used and years searched per section, please see Appendix 1. --- Chunk 73 ---
Clinical practice guidelines provide recommenda- tions applicable to patients with or at risk of developing cardiovascular disease (CVD). The focus is on medical practice in the United States, but these guidelines are relevant to patients throughout the world. Although guidelines may be used to inform regulatory or payer decisions, the goals are to improve quality of care and align with patients’ interests. Guidelines are intended to define practices meeting the needs of patients in most but not all circumstances and should not replace clinical judgment.

4.4. Adults With High Blood Pressure or Hypertension Recommendations from the 2017 Hypertension Clinical Practice GuidelinesS4.4-1 are adapted below.

Primary ASCVD prevention requires attention to AS- CVD risk factors beginning early in life (Figure 3). The benefit from statin therapy is related to both global risk and intensity of treatment,S4.3-2 and no RCTs of high- intensity statin therapy have been carried out in cohorts of patients exclusively with diabetes. On the basis of these considerations and the fact that patients with dia- betes have a higher trajectory of lifetime risk than do those without diabetes, high-intensity statin therapy is preferred in patients with diabetes as they develop risk modifiers (Table 5).

Beginning in 2017, numerous modifications to the guidelines have been and continue to be implemented to make guidelines shorter and enhance “user friendli- ness.” Guidelines are written and presented in a modu- lar knowledge chunk format, in which each chunk in- cludes a table of recommendations, a brief synopsis, recommendation-specific supportive text and, when appropriate, flow diagrams or additional tables. Hyper- linked references are provided for each modular knowl- edge chunk to facilitate quick access and review. More structured guidelines—including word limits (“tar- gets”) and a web guideline supplement for useful but noncritical tables and figures—are 2 such changes. This Preamble is an abbreviated version, with the detailed version available online.

--- Chunk 136 ---
The incorporation of the value category into clinical practice guidelines is one of several considerations in medical decision-making and resource allocation. Clini- cians, researchers, and policymakers alike must contin- ue to place cost-effective analyses in the proper context, extracting key value determinations while acknowledg- ing the challenges in fully characterizing and incorpo- rating the downstream benefits of a given therapeutic prevention tactic. Further research and methodological advances are needed to comprehensively characterize the full spectrum of benefits produced by the preven- tion approach, thereby rendering cost-effectiveness as- sessments more consequential to clinical practice.

--- Chunk 143 ---
Prevention strategies occur at the population level but must also engage individual adults to slow the de- velopment of ASCVD. The most important way to pre- vent ASCVD is to promote a healthy lifestyle through- out life. Prevention strategies must include a strong focus on lifestyle optimization (improvements in diet, physical activity, and avoidance of tobacco use and ex- posure to secondhand smoke) to minimize the risk of future ASCVD events.

Patrick T. O’Gara, MD, MACC, FAHA Chair, ACC/AHA Task Force on Clinical Practice Guidelines

A comprehensive patient-centered approach that addresses all aspects of a patient’s lifestyle habits and estimated risk of a future ASCVD event is the first step in deciding on where there may be a need for pharmacotherapy. Even if a blood pressure (BP)–reduc- ing medication, lipid-lowering medication, or diabe- tes medication is ultimately prescribed, lifestyle goals should be emphasized on a regular basis. Populations From African Descent

Black populations, whether residing in Africa, the Caribbean, United States, or Europe, develop hy- pertension and associated organ damage at younger ages, have a higher frequency of resistant and night- time hypertension, and a higher risk of kidney di- sease,131 stroke, HF, and mortality,132 than other eth- nic groups.

--- Chunk 3 ---
Laboratory Investigations and ECG

Blood tests: Sodium, potassium, serum creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). If a- vailable, lipid profile and fasting glucose.

A reliable estimate of cardiovascular risk can be ob- tained in daily practice by including:

Urine test: Dipstick urine test. • 12-lead ECG: Detection of atrial fibrillation, left ven- tricular hypertrophy (LVH), ischemic heart disease.

Other Risk Factors: Age

(>65 years), sex (male>female), heart rate (>80 beats/min), increased body weight, diabetes, high LDL-C/triglyceride, fam- ily history of CVD, family history of hypertension, early-onset menopause, smoking habits, psychosocial or socioeconomic factors. HMOD: LVH (LVH with ECG), moderate-severe CKD (CKD; eGFR <60 ml/ min/1.73m2), any other available measure of organ damage. Disease: previous coronary heart disease (CHD), HF, stroke, peripheral vascular disease, atrial fibrillation, CKD stage 3+.

--- Chunk 14 ---
Healthy drinks

Moderate consumption of coffee, green and black tea.50 Other beverages that can be beneficial include karkadé (hibiscus) tea, pomegranate juice, beetroot juice and cocoa.49

Moderation of alcohol consumption

Positive linear association exists between alcohol consumption, blood pressure, the prevalence of hypertension, and CVD risk.51 The recommended daily limit for alcohol consumptions is 2 standard drinks for men and 1.5 for women (10 g alcohol/standard drink). Avoid binge drinking.

Body weight control is indicated to avoid obesity. Particularly abdominal obesity should be managed. Ethnic-specific cut-offs for BMI and waist circumference should be used.52 Alternatively, a waist-to-height ratio <0.5 is recommended for all populations.53,54

Prevention of Preeclampsia Women at high risk (hypertension in previous pregnancy, CKD, autoimmune disease, diabetes, chronic hypertension), or moderate risk (first pregnancy in a woman >40 years, pregnancy interval >10 years, BMI >35 kg/m2, family his- tory of preeclampsia, multiple pregnancies): 75–162 mg aspirin at weeks 12–36. Oral calcium supplementation of 1.5–2 g/day is recommended in women with low dietary in- take (<600 mg/day).

Malignant hypertension: Severe BP elevation (com- monly >200/120 mm Hg) associated with advanced bilateral retinopathy (hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, papilledema).

Hypertensive encephalopathy: Severe BP elevation associated with lethargy, seizures, cortical blindness and coma in the absence of other explanations.

Hypertensive thrombotic microangiopathy: Severe BP elevation associated with hemolysis and thrombocy- topenia in the absence of other causes and improvement with BP-lowering therapy.

--- Chunk 27 ---
Isolated systolic hypertension defined as elevated SBP (≥140 mm Hg) and low DBP (<90 mm Hg) is common in young and in elderly people. In young individuals, including children, adolescents and young adults, iso- lated systolic hypertension is the most common form of essential hypertension. However, it is also particularly common in the elderly, in whom it reflects stiffening of the large arteries with an increase in pulse pressure (dif- ference between SBP and DBP).

Hypertension and Previous Stroke

Hypertension is the most important risk factor for ische- mic or hemorrhagic stroke.90

combinations

Stroke can be largely prevented by BP control. • BP should be lowered if ≥140/90 mm Hg and treated to a target <130/80 mm Hg (<140/80 in elderly patients).1 • RAS blockers, CCBs, and diuretics are first-line drugs. 1 • Lipid-lowering treatment is mandatory with a LDL-C target <70 mg/dL (1.8 mmol/L) in ischemic stroke.1 • Antiplatelet treatment is routinely recommended for is- chemic stroke, but not hemorrhagic stroke, and should be carefully considered in patients with hemorrhagic stroke only in the presence of a strong indication.1

--- Chunk 39 ---
10.4 Hypertensive Emergencies

Definition of Hypertensive Emergencies and Their Clinical Presentation A hypertensive emergency is the association of substantially elevated BP with acute HMOD. Target organs include the retina, brain, heart, large arteries, and the kidneys.127 This situation requires rapid diagnostic workup and immediate BP reduction to avoid progressive organ failure. Intravenous therapy is usually required. The choice of antihypertensive treatment is predominantly determined by the type of organ damage. Specific clinical presentations of hypertensive emer - gencies include:

Ultrasound of kidneys and adrenals, free plasma metanephrines (if clinical features of pheochromocytoma); Doppler ultrasound of uterine arteries (after 20 weeks of gestation is useful to detect those at higher risk of gesta- tional hypertension, preeclampsia, and intrauterine growth retardation).

--- Chunk 55 ---
Interpretation

White coat hypertension: These subjects are at inter- mediate cardiovascular risk between normotensives and sustained hypertensives. The diagnosis needs confirma- tion with repeated office and out-of-office BP measure- ments. If their total cardiovascular risk is low and there is no hypertension-mediated organ damage (HMOD), drug treatment may not be prescribed. However, they should be followed with lifestyle modification, as they

may develop sustained hypertension requiring drug treatment.1,2,17–21,25–27

Masked hypertension: These patients are at similar risk of cardiovascular events as sustained hypertensives. The diagnosis needs confirmation with repeated office and out-of-office measurements. Masked hypertension may require drug treatment aiming to normalize out-of-office BP.1,2,17–21,25–27 Section 4: Diagnostic / Clinical Tests
